title: QUIC RFC 9000 S9P6P1 Preferred Address Handshake-Confirmed Transition
purpose: Describe the focused S9P6P1 closure for client preferred-address selection, validation, and cutover after handshake confirmation.
design_summary: Client HANDSHAKE_DONE processing confirms the handshake and starts validation for a usable server preferred_address candidate. The runtime selects the address family matching the active path when possible, falls back to the other usable family when the active family is unused, sends a PATH_CHALLENGE to the selected preferred address, and keeps the original server address active until validation succeeds.
data_and_state_considerations: The preferred-address candidate is tracked as an unvalidated candidate path. Because the client originates validation to a server-advertised address, the candidate receives send budget for its validation probe without marking path validation complete. Existing path-validation success handling then records the preferred path as validated, promotes it as the active send path, and prevents continued use of the old server address for the preferred-address migration.
edge_cases_and_constraints: No preferred_address transport parameter means HANDSHAKE_DONE confirmation does not create a preferred-address candidate.
An all-zero or zero-port address family is skipped, with fallback to the other usable family.
IPv6 active paths select the IPv6 preferred address when that family is usable.
The old server address remains active while preferred-address validation is pending.
risks: This slice does not add public migration controls.
This slice does not add multipath scheduling.
This slice does not close deferred fuzz obligations for S9P6P1.

supplemental_sections.heading: Boundary
supplemental_sections.content: This design closes the S9P6P1 preferred-address handshake-confirmed transition for REQ-QUIC-RFC9000-S9P6P1-0002, REQ-QUIC-RFC9000-S9P6P1-0003, REQ-QUIC-RFC9000-S9P6P1-0004, and REQ-QUIC-RFC9000-0525 only. It does not claim complete S9P6P1 closure, preferred-address failure-policy proof, server preferred_address emission proof, public API widening, multipath support, hosted interop readiness, or closure of deferred fuzz obligations.
